headline: Oil price surge is a supply shock, not demand-driven — acts as a deflationary force medium-term by destroying consumer demand
reasoning: Canavan contends that the spike in oil and energy prices is supply-driven rather than a reflection of strong demand, which means it should be treated as a deflationary force over the medium term. Higher energy prices remove money from consumers' pockets, reducing spending on other goods and services. While businesses will try to pass on costs, demand destruction is likely. He also notes that refined products (petrol, diesel, gas) are particularly constrained even though crude supply is adequate.
quote: I've always argued that supply shocks in the energy sector, they're not demand driven. This is a supply reason why oil prices are heading higher. This is not because of strong demand. So that's actually can be a deflationary force if you look through the short term impact of flowing through to inflation because those higher energy prices take money out of people's pockets. So it's less money available to spend on other things. Now businesses will obviously try to pass those costs through, but there comes a point where it's going to hurt demand. And I think we're probably not far off seeing that.

headline: Bond yield surge is driven by strong nominal growth (AI boom + government spending), not just inflation fears — negativity towards bonds looks overdone in the short term
reasoning: Greg Canavan argues that the dominant narrative of bond yields rising due to inflation fears is only part of the story. Strong nominal economic growth, driven by the AI boom and aggressive government spending, is a key force pushing yields higher. He views the current hysteria around bond yields as excessive and analogous to capitulation signals seen in equity markets. In the short term, he expects central bank rate hikes (including the Fed at its September 16 meeting) to eventually knock growth on the head and cause long-end yields to turn lower, which would signal that inflation worries are overblown.
quote: I think it's exactly that because nominal economic growth around the world has been so strong and that's been driven by the AI boom as well as governments that are spending very, very fast and consistently as well. And those two forces are coming together to push bond yields higher and it's also pushing economic growth higher. So I don't think it's a reason to sort of panic too much about what these bond yields mean. But one concern I do have is that, you know, we're seeing a lot of hysteria, a lot of headlines in the media over the past couple of days about bond yields... I look at the psychological state of markets and if this was an equity market that had been falling all year and then we see these headlines out saying, you know, existential crisis for equity markets, would that would mean we're pretty close to a bottom. I'm not saying that we're close to a long term bottom. I think longer term we do have some issues with inflation, with lack of productivity, with huge amounts of spending going on. But certainly in the short term, it feels like this negativity towards bonds is probably overdone.

headline: Australian equity market broadly overvalued — housing turning into structural downturn, productivity absent, RBA likely to hike, risks being ignored
reasoning: Canavan sees a meaningful disconnect in Australia between equity market pricing and underlying fundamentals. The housing market is turning down in what he expects to be a structural, prolonged downturn. There is no productivity growth and the tax and regulatory settings to improve it are absent. Even modest economic growth is generating inflation, forcing the RBA to raise rates. He concludes the market is broadly overvalued on a risk-return basis and that investors need to look at individual stocks to find value.
quote: We've got a housing market that is turning down and it's looking like it's going to be a structural downturn, which means it's going to be around for some time. We have got a lack of productivity growth. We don't have any of the tax settings or the regulatory settings to increase productivity, which we really need. So even a bit of growth that comes through in the economy and we saw some reasonably decent numbers today. They weren't great, but that's creating inflation and the Reserve Bank is going to have to raise interest rates. So to me, the equity market is very much ignoring these risks. And when you look at it on a risk return basis, I think the market is very much overvalued here. And you really need to look at individual stocks to see value.
